interactions.label: A 38-year-old woman undergoes breast biopsy showing atypical ductal hyperplasia.

params.question: A 38-year-old woman undergoes breast biopsy showing atypical ductal hyperplasia. Her mother was diagnosed with breast carcinoma at age 45. What is her approximate relative risk of developing breast cancer?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 1.5–2× risk applies to proliferative lesions WITHOUT atypia, such as usual ductal hyperplasia or sclerosing adenosis.
A 4–5× risk applies to atypical hyperplasia WITHOUT a family history. The positive family history in this patient further escalates the risk.
Correct. Atypical hyperplasia (4–5× alone) combined with a positive family history raises the relative risk to 8–10 times baseline — the highest benign-category risk recognised.
This figure is not part of the Page & Dupont classification. The highest benign-category risk (atypia + family history) reaches 8–10×, not 15–20×.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Page & Dupont classification: non-proliferative = no increase, proliferative without atypia = 1.5–2×, proliferative with atypia = 4–5×, and atypia plus family history = 8–10× baseline.
Excellent. Atypical hyperplasia plus family history is the highest-risk benign combination, reaching 8–10× baseline — a figure that often triggers enhanced screening or risk-reducing strategies.

interactions.label: The fibrous phase of gynecomastia shows ductal hyperplasia with oedematous perid

params.question: The fibrous phase of gynecomastia shows ductal hyperplasia with oedematous periductal stroma and is reversible with treatment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The description given (ductal hyperplasia with oedematous stroma, reversible) describes the FLORID phase, not the fibrous phase. The FIBROUS phase shows dense hyalinised periductal fibrosis and is irreversible. Only florid-phase gynecomastia regresses with medical treatment.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The description given (ductal hyperplasia with oedematous stroma, reversible) actually describes the FLORID phase. The fibrous phase shows dense hyalinised periductal fibrosis and is irreversible — an important distinction for surgical planning.

params.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) from ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)?

answers.text: LCIS shows comedo-type necrosis with linear microcalcifications on mammography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Comedo-type necrosis with linear and branching microcalcifications is characteristic of DCIS (comedo subtype), not LCIS.

answers.text: LCIS is treated with wide local excision and adjuvant radiation therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Excision and radiation is the standard approach for DCIS. LCIS is a bilateral risk marker managed with surveillance, not surgery.

answers.text: LCIS cells lose E-cadherin expression and the lesion is managed with surveillance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. E-cadherin loss explains the discohesive, scattered appearance of LCIS cells. Unlike DCIS (a localised precursor treated surgically), LCIS is a bilateral risk marker managed with surveillance.

answers.text: LCIS carries a higher risk of progression to invasive carcinoma than comedo-type DCIS

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Comedo-type DCIS carries the highest risk of progression to invasive carcinoma among in situ lesions, particularly when HER2 is amplified. LCIS confers bilateral risk but has a lower progression rate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: DCIS is a localised precursor (excision ± radiation), while LCIS shows E-cadherin loss, discohesive cells, and bilateral risk — managed with surveillance, not surgery.
Well done. The E-cadherin loss → discohesive cells → bilateral risk marker → surveillance pathway is a key molecular-to-management chain in breast pathology.

params.question: A 48-year-old woman undergoes modified radical mastectomy. Her tumour is 1.8 cm, Nottingham Grade 2, oestrogen-receptor positive, and HER2-negative. Three of fifteen axillary lymph nodes contain metastatic deposits. Which factor among these carries the greatest prognostic weight?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tumour size is an important prognostic factor and determines T-stage, but it is not the single strongest predictor of outcome in breast carcinoma.
Histological grade (based on tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic count) is prognostically significant but ranks below axillary node status.
This Luminal A molecular profile carries a favourable prognosis and guides treatment choice, but molecular subtype is not the single strongest prognostic factor.

answers.text: Axillary lymph node metastasis in 3 of 15 nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Axillary lymph node status is the single strongest prognostic factor in breast carcinoma. Three positive nodes out of fifteen places this patient at significantly higher risk of recurrence despite otherwise favourable tumour features.

overallFeedback.feedback: While all four factors are prognostically important, axillary lymph node status is the single strongest prognostic factor in breast carcinoma. Tumour size, grade, and molecular subtype complete the top four.
Exactly. Axillary node status trumps tumour size, histological grade, and molecular subtype as the single strongest prognostic determinant in breast carcinoma.

interactions.label: A breast biopsy shows malignant epithelial cells filling a duct. The pathologist

params.question: A breast biopsy shows malignant epithelial cells filling a duct. The pathologist must determine whether this is in situ or invasive disease. Which single histological feature is the most reliable discriminator?

answers.text: Degree of nuclear pleomorphism in the malignant cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nuclear pleomorphism indicates grade, not invasion. Both in situ and invasive carcinomas can show high-grade pleomorphism.

answers.text: Presence of central comedo-type necrosis within the duct

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Comedo-type necrosis is characteristic of high-grade DCIS but does not by itself indicate invasion. Invasion is defined by breach of the basement membrane.

answers.text: Integrity of the basement membrane and myoepithelial layer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An intact basement membrane with preserved myoepithelial cells defines in situ disease. Loss of the myoepithelial layer and breach of the basement membrane define invasion — the critical line between DCIS and invasive ductal carcinoma.

answers.text: Density of the surrounding desmoplastic stromal reaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Desmoplastic stroma is characteristic of invasive ductal carcinoma but is a secondary feature. The primary discriminator is the status of the basement membrane and myoepithelial layer.

overallFeedback.feedback: The defining feature of invasion is breach of the basement membrane with loss of the myoepithelial layer. Myoepithelial presence = benign or in situ; myoepithelial loss = invasive. This is the fundamental diagnostic line.
Precisely. The basement membrane and its myoepithelial cell lining are the pathologist's two key discriminators — their preservation means in situ disease; their loss means invasion.
